### Sandbox price increases come with notice too

You say to your agent

> “Will sandbox prices go up while my rollouts run?”

A sandbox rate increase now also comes at least 24 hours before it takes effect, and we tell you about it. That is any higher rate: active sandboxes, parked sandboxes and snapshots, or cold snapshots.

The dashboard shows a notice until a few days after the increase takes effect. The admins and billing members of each organization that used sandboxes in the last 90 days get an email. A new rate applies to each billing hour that starts at or after that time. See Rates.

### We tell you about a price increase before it takes effect

You say to your agent

> “Is the price of an H100 going to change soon?”

A price increase now always comes at least 24 hours before it takes effect, and we tell you about it. An increase is a higher list price, or a smaller Friday, weekend, or batch job discount.

When we schedule an increase, the dashboard shows a notice until a few days after it takes effect. The admins and billing members of each organization that used that type in the last 90 days get an email.

Your agent sees it too. Until the increase takes effect, `create_node` and `get_node` carry it in `rate.upcoming_increase`, and `submit_job` carries it in `upcoming_increase`. The field gives the time it takes effect, the new list rate per GPU and per node, and the new discounts. A running node also gets a `price_change` event on `/v1/events`. See Rates.

...

## October 8, 2026

1. 07:00 UTC

### The H100 price is now $5.04 per GPU-hour

On October 8 at 00:00 Pacific time, the H100 list price changed from $3.96 to $5.04 per GPU-hour. Per GPU-minute, the price changed from $0.066 to $0.084. A whole 8-GPU node now costs $40.32 per hour.

The new price applies to each minute that we bill from that time. This includes the minutes of nodes and jobs that were already running. Minutes before that time bill at the old price.

The discounts did not change, and they now apply to the new list price. Friday hours are 33% off, and Saturday and Sunday hours are 20% off, on the Pacific calendar. Batch jobs are 25% off the list price. The docs show the rates.

We did not tell you about this change before it took effect. We are sorry for the late notice. If you have a question about your bill, send it to us on the contact page.

...

### A receipt on every finished job

You say to your agent

> “That eval finished. What image did it actually run, and what did it cost?”

A finished job now carries a `receipt`. `image_digest` is the manifest digest we resolved and pinned for the run. Beside it are `billed_seconds`, `charged_usd_micros`, and one row per billed attempt with the rate it billed at. These come from the same billing records your invoice totals to, so you get a result and its price in one lookup. The digest was not available before this, and the cost was only in a usage report for a date range.

```
gman job get job-8x2mf
→ ... "receipt": {"image_digest": "sha256:70d6845739d5...",
                  "billed_seconds": 10650, "billed_attempts": 1,
                  "charged_usd_micros": 8866, "attempts": [...]}
```

Billed seconds are the seconds for one GPU. The charge is seconds x `gpu_count` x rate / 60. An attempt we cut short, such as a preemption, bills only the progress that survived. It bills nothing unless it had checkpointed. A shorter list is the free attempts rather than a gap.

A billing fix ships with it. ... The attempt now closes at the deadline you bought, and never later. You do not pay for our own enforcement running late. ... See the docs.

results.title: Standard Intelligence and Roboflow access larger GPU clusters through SF Compute’s resale market | SF Compute
highlights:
# Standard Intelligence and Roboflow access larger GPU clusters through SF Compute’s resale market#

September 28, 2026

Standard Intelligence and Roboflow scale with SF Compute

Mason Wheeler

SF Compute helps companies afford larger GPU clusters by letting them resell GPU hours to other teams. Customers can reserve enough GPUs for their biggest workloads, keep the hours they need, and sell unused hours to help reduce the reservation cost.

Those resold hours become short-term reservations for other teams, giving them access to large clusters for individual jobs without a long-term commitment.

## Standard Intelligence#

Standard Intelligence builds frontier models that learn from video to carry out computer tasks. They resell GPU hours outside of peak usage periods, which allows them to purchase larger, interconnected clusters to serve their most demanding workloads.

> “We procure compute calibrated to our peak load rather than the average. Because our cluster on SF Compute is supported by a resale market with high liquidity, the cost to hold excess capacity is just the small delta from price fluctuations, rather than the entire value of the underlying contract. This means we get larger scaleups while having lower baseline spend than traditional clouds.”

Galen Mead CEO

## Roboflow#

Resale from customers like Standard Intelligence makes more GPU capacity available for teams that need shorter commitments.

Roboflow, a computer vision startup, buys short-term GPU reservations on SF Compute. Their teams can run larger jobs and reserve just the time each job needs.

> “SF Compute lets us take on bigger workloads with shorter commitments. Through the market, we can access larger clusters for the time we need them and match our reservations to the jobs we want to run.”

Isaac Robinson Research Lead

## A new model for compute providers#

In a traditional anchor tenant model, one customer makes a long-term commitment to a cluster at a fixed price. The provider earns the agreed contract revenue, regardless of how much of that capacity the customer uses.

Traditional Anchor Tenant Model

Long-term contract One long-term commitment

With SF Compute, that same commitment can generate an additional source of revenue. When the anchor tenant resells GPU hours to other teams, the provider earns a share of the resale fees on top of the original contract revenue.

SF Compute lets providers offer long-term anchor contracts, short-term burst contracts, or both. Shorter reservations can command higher hourly rates while costing customers less overall. Both contract types let customers resell GPU hours, with providers earning a share of resale fees on top of contract revenue.

Powered by SF Compute

Anchor tenant + resale One long-term commitment with resale to other tenants

Short-term burst + resale Multiple tenants over time

results.title: San Francisco Compute's Evan Conrad wants to build a utility-grade compute market — starting with the biggest supercomputer ever | TBPN Digest
results.author: Evan Conrad
highlights:
## Key Points

- San Francisco Compute is positioning itself as a grid operator for AI compute, arguing the market needs a utility layer with independent operators and physical settlement, not just synthetic futures contracts.
- Conrad identifies supercomputing expertise as the bottleneck holding back standardization, with only a handful of qualified operators like CoreWeave and Nebius capable of running infrastructure at scale.
- A liquid forward market for GPU pricing would eliminate large upfront deposits that force AI labs to raise capital at inflated valuations, compressing venture valuation inflation currently embedded in the stack.

...

### The San Francisco Compute model

Conrad's solution has two parts. First, an independent market operator — independence being the prerequisite for Wall Street to trust the infrastructure. Second, physical settlement, meaning the operator doesn't just clear contracts but actually runs the compute, down to the data center level. In Conrad's framing, you can't standardize a market if you don't control the technology underneath it.

The hyperscalers aren't the target or the enemy. He frames them as the factories and the neo-clouds as their generators — useful relationships, but not a market. What's missing is a utility layer above them that lets new capital enter, derisk compute investments, and price GPU capacity forward. San Francisco Compute wants to be that layer, helping new operators become clouds and then placing them on the market.

### Where the bubble actually sits

On the overbuild question, Conrad offers a specific mechanism. Clouds won't deploy a GPU cluster until they have a signed customer contract, and they require a large upfront deposit to pass through to the OEM and then to Nvidia. The AI lab paying that deposit doesn't have the capital yet, so it raises at a high valuation. VCs, scarred by missing OpenAI and Anthropic, accept the valuation. The risk, Conrad argues, lands with the venture capitalists — not distributed across a functioning market.

San Francisco Compute's solution is to make future GPU pricing knowable, which removes the need for the large upfront deposit, which in turn reduces pressure on AI labs to raise at stretched valuations. Conrad is essentially arguing that a liquid forward market for compute would compress the valuation inflation currently baked into the VC stack.

...

Conrad confirms the company is targeting "the biggest computer ever" and says a data center build-out is in progress, though specifics aren't disclosed. He describes San Francisco Compute as a "supercomputer developer" that helps capital-rich operators become neo-clouds, then finances them through the market it's building.

The bet is that every dollar of capital currently trying to convert itself into GPUs needs infrastructure to do so competently. If Conrad is right that expertise is the bottleneck, a credible operator-developer hybrid that can raise the floor across the market is the right place to be.

results.title: Rental Rates for Older AI Chips Jump 25% as Demand Surges - Seoul Economic Daily
results.author: Seo Ji-hye, Kim Ji-young
highlights:
17:52:17

...

Vessl AI raised its hourly rate for Nvidia H100 graphics processing units by 24.7% starting this month, following a string of price increases by U.S. neocloud providers such as CoreWeave and Nebius amid a surge in demand for artificial intelligence computing. Supply has tightened not only for the newest chips but also for older models as demand for high-performance GPUs jumps. Other Korean cloud providers also expect to raise GPU rates depending on supply conditions, raising concerns that higher costs of securing GPUs will weigh on service development at Korean AI companies and on government AI transformation, or AX, projects.

Vessl AI on the 1st raised the hourly rate for H100 chips on its VESSL Cloud service to $2.98 from $2.39, according to AI industry sources on the 21st. The neocloud company counts leading Korean AI firms including Upstage and Motif Technologies among its clients and currently operates several thousand GPUs. It has secured about 7,000 GPUs, most of them leased rather than purchased outright. "It is hard to secure the volume we need for H100s — effectively, the price is whatever the seller names," a Vessl AI official said. "As AI demand grows, the number of customers wanting to use GPUs keeps rising, so a price adjustment was unavoidable." The company plans to expand its GPU fleet to about 10,000 units by the end of the year, but intends to keep adjusting rates flexibly to reflect supply conditions and procurement costs.

Other Korean AI cloud companies, including Elice, have also raised prices recently. In the past, rental rates for older AI GPUs fell when new models arrived, but prices for previous-generation chips are now rising as well. Hourly cloud rental rates for the H100 climbed 21.9% over the past month to $3.28 from $2.69, according to Ornn, an AI compute trading platform. That is about 70% of the price of the higher-end H200. Analysts say demand is spilling over to relatively older GPUs because supply of the newest chips cannot keep pace with surging computing demand.

The trend is affecting Korea's AI industry and research community. Some companies have given up bidding for government AX projects because they could not secure the GPUs they needed. Universities and research institutes, unable to obtain GPUs reliably, are scaling back research or searching for new funding programs. "What determines success or failure in business and research now is not just whether you have good AI technology, but whether you can secure the GPUs you need in time," an AI industry official said. "The ability to secure computing resources is becoming a key element of AI competitiveness."
